name: Scheduled Task/Job
overview: Every major platform ships a way to run code on a schedule rather than once, and adversaries use exactly that legitimate capability to make execution survive a reboot, a logoff, or the original delivery vector being cleaned up entirely. MITRE lists this technique under three tactics at once — Execution, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation — because a scheduled task doesn't just guarantee code runs again later, it can also run under a more privileged context than the account that scheduled it. The 5 sub-techniques below split by platform and scheduler: Windows Task Scheduler and the legacy at utility, Linux/macOS/ESXi cron, Linux systemd timers, and Kubernetes CronJobs for containerized environments.

prerequisite_concepts.term: Recurring execution is the actual value, not the delay
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: A one-time delayed execution is barely more useful to an attacker than running immediately. What makes scheduling worth the effort is recurrence and reboot-survival: a task that fires every few minutes, or specifically at startup, keeps re-establishing a foothold even after the host is patched, the user logs off, or the original phishing payload is deleted from disk. Every sub-technique in this pack is really being hunted for its persistence value, not its scheduling mechanics.

prerequisite_concepts.term: The universal shape: a definition plus a trigger
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: Every scheduler covered here splits 'what to run' from 'when to run it' into two linked artifacts — a Windows scheduled task's action and trigger, a crontab line's command and time fields, a systemd .service paired with a .timer, a Kubernetes Job template paired with a CronJob's schedule. That consistent shape is exactly why detection has to correlate both halves: a hunt that only watches for new task/unit/crontab creation without also checking what it actually runs will miss the part that tells you whether it's malicious.

prerequisite_concepts.term: Why this is a privilege-escalation vector, not just persistence
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: Several of these mechanisms let a task execute under a more privileged context than the user who scheduled it — a Windows task set to run as SYSTEM, a cron job dropped by a low-privilege web shell into a root-owned crontab, a Kubernetes CronJob whose pod spec requests a privileged container. Scheduling something is often the easy part; getting it to run as someone more powerful than you is the actual objective, which is why this technique sits under Privilege Escalation as much as Persistence.

prerequisite_concepts.term: Hiding from the tool's own management interface, not just from logs
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: Windows Task Scheduler specifically can be made to hide a task from both the Task Scheduler GUI and schtasks /query by deleting or corrupting its Security Descriptor registry value, while the task keeps running exactly as scheduled underneath. That means 'the task doesn't show up when I look' is not the same as 'the task doesn't exist' — a hunt has to check the underlying registry/filesystem artifacts directly rather than trusting each scheduler's own enumeration tooling.

subtechniques.name: At
subtechniques.overview: The at utility schedules one-time or recurring execution on Windows, Linux, and macOS alike. Microsoft deprecated it on Windows in favor of schtasks, but at.exe still ships and still works, internally creating its job through the same Task Scheduler subsystem. On Linux/macOS, whether a non-root user can use it at all is governed by the at.allow and at.deny files.

concepts.term: Deprecated doesn't mean gone, or unmonitored
concepts.explanation: Windows keeps shipping at.exe for backward compatibility even though schtasks and the Task Scheduler GUI are the documented modern path. Precisely because it's legacy and less commonly used by legitimate administrators, at.exe activity draws less routine scrutiny than schtasks does in most environments — which is exactly why it still shows up in real intrusions despite being the 'old' way to do this.

concepts.term: at.allow / at.deny as the access gate on Linux/macOS
concepts.explanation: Unlike cron, which uses its own separate cron.allow/cron.deny pair, at gates access through its own at.allow/at.deny files. If neither file exists on a given host, only the superuser can schedule an at job at all — which means on a default-configured Linux host, any at job's mere existence already implies root-level access was used to create it, regardless of who the job appears to belong to.

procedure_examples.activity: Used the native Windows at task scheduler tool for execution on a victim network.
Employed at to register scheduled tasks executing malware during lateral movement.
Utilized at to schedule tasks running self-extracting RAR archives that installed HTTPBrowser or PlugX.
Capable of setting scheduled tasks via at for remote command execution.

data_sources.detail: HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\TaskCache\Tree\At1 and similarly-numbered keys, created when at.exe registers a job.
at.exe process creation with its schedule and command arguments.
atd job execution, and modification of /etc/at.allow or /etc/at.deny themselves, which is itself worth watching.

detection_queries.title: at.exe Execution on Windows

status: stable
author: H3AD-SEC Detection Engineering
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\at.exe'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legacy scripts or documentation that still reference at.exe in environments that haven't fully migrated to schtasks
level: medium
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - attack.t1053.002

false_positives: Legacy administrative scripts in environments that haven't fully migrated off at.exe to schtasks
Rare legitimate Linux/macOS batch-processing workflows still using at instead of cron for one-off delayed jobs
response_steps: Identify the scheduled command and confirm it against any legitimate change record
On Linux/macOS, check whether at.allow/at.deny exist and who they permit, since their absence implies root-level creation
Remove the job and check for the same TaskCache registry pattern on other hosts if this was pushed via a shared script

mitigations.name: Operating System Configuration
mitigations.detail: Force tasks to run under an authenticated account context rather than SYSTEM where possible; disable server-operator scheduling via Group Policy.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Restrict scheduling-priority rights to the Administrators group.

mitigations.name: User Account Management
mitigations.detail: Limit which users can schedule tasks; manage Linux/macOS access explicitly via at.allow/at.deny.

related.name: Scheduled Task
related.relation: The modern, actively-maintained Windows scheduling mechanism at.exe was deprecated in favor of.

hypothesis.statement: at.exe executes on a Windows host, or an at job is scheduled on a Linux/macOS host where neither at.allow nor at.deny exists.
hypothesis.rationale: Because schtasks is the documented modern path on Windows, any at.exe execution in an environment that has standardized on it is itself an anomaly worth a look, independent of what the job actually runs.

subtechniques.name: Cron
subtechniques.overview: cron reads scheduling entries from crontab files — per-user and system-wide — and executes the associated command at each specified interval. On ESXi specifically, there's no friendly per-user crontab command; an attacker with root edits /var/spool/cron/crontabs/root directly to add a job.

concepts.term: @reboot: the persistence-specific trigger malware actually wants
concepts.explanation: Alongside standard interval scheduling, cron supports a special @reboot string that runs a job exactly once at system startup rather than repeatedly. That's precisely the trigger malware authors reach for, since it guarantees re-execution after every restart without needing a real recurring interval that might draw attention through sheer execution frequency.

concepts.term: Why ESXi cron abuse is unusually quiet
concepts.explanation: Standard Linux cron abuse at least involves invoking the crontab command, which is itself a process-creation event to catch. ESXi's cron implementation instead expects direct edits to a single root-owned crontab file — an attacker with root can modify /var/spool/cron/crontabs/root with any text editor or even a redirect, with no crontab utility invocation to catch at all. The file write is the only signal; there's no command execution to correlate against.

procedure_examples.activity: Installs cron jobs downloading and executing cryptomining files from attacker infrastructure.
Downloads and executes shell scripts via crontab entries running every minute.
Employs crontab entries with @reboot for execution at system startup.
Modifies crontab files, including entries under /var/cron/tabs/.
Creates cron jobs for Linux persistence as part of its worming behavior.

data_sources.detail: Writes to /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d/, /etc/cron.allow, /etc/cron.deny, or any user's crontab file, especially by a process other than the crontab binary itself.
cron itself logs every job execution with a CRON tag, which is the most direct record of what actually ran and when, independent of how the crontab entry was created.
Direct modification timestamps on /var/spool/cron/crontabs/root, correlated against auth.log for the session that touched it.

detection_queries.title: Crontab Modification by Non-Interactive or Unexpected Process
detection_queries.description: Flags crontab file changes made by something other than the crontab utility itself, a common pattern for scripted/malware-driven persistence.
detection_queries.query:
title: Crontab Modified by Unexpected Process

mitigations.name: Audit
mitigations.detail: Monitor /var/log for cron schedule changes; verify syslog is actually capturing CRON execution entries.

mitigations.name: User Account Management
mitigations.detail: Control cron access explicitly via /etc/cron.allow and /etc/cron.deny.

related.name: Systemd Timers
related.relation: The more modern Linux scheduling alternative to cron, increasingly seen alongside or instead of it.

related.name: Unix Shell
related.relation: The command a malicious cron entry almost always ultimately invokes.

hypothesis.statement: A crontab file (/etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d/*, or a user/root crontab) is modified by a process other than the crontab binary itself, or a new entry uses the @reboot trigger.
hypothesis.rationale: Scope the initial hunt to the @reboot trigger specifically if volume is a concern -- it's a much smaller, higher-signal subset than all crontab changes, since legitimate recurring maintenance jobs rarely need to fire at startup specifically.

subtechniques.name: Scheduled Task
subtechniques.overview: Windows Task Scheduler is reachable via the schtasks command line, the Task Scheduler GUI, COM/WMI, .NET wrappers, or PowerShell's Invoke-CimMethod against the PS_ScheduledTask WMI class. Adversaries use it for persistence (run at logon or on an interval), lateral movement (schedule execution on a remote host using stolen credentials), and privilege escalation (a task configured to run as SYSTEM).

concepts.term: Two logs, both off by default
concepts.explanation: Security 4698 (task created) requires the 'Audit Other Object Access Events' subcategory to be explicitly enabled — it isn't on by default. The Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational log tells a richer story (106 created, 140 updated, 141 deleted, 200 executed, 201 execution completed) but also isn't audited out of the box. In practice, most environments have neither turned on until someone deliberately does it, which is worth confirming before assuming this technique is already covered by existing logging.

concepts.term: Hiding a task from its own management tools
concepts.explanation: Deleting or corrupting a task's Security Descriptor (SD) registry value under the Task Scheduler's own registry tree makes that task invisible to both the Task Scheduler GUI and schtasks /query, while it continues to fire exactly as scheduled underneath. This is a distinctly Windows-specific evasion trick with no equivalent among cron, systemd timers, or Kubernetes CronJobs — none of those schedulers have an analogous 'hide from your own enumeration tool' registry knob.

concepts.term: A COM handler action has no command line to inspect at all
concepts.explanation: Task Scheduler supports a second action type beyond "run this program": invoking a registered COM object by CLSID instead. Neither schtasks.exe's own output nor the Task Scheduler GUI (which just labels it "Custom Handler") shows what that COM handler actually does, and because there's no executable path or command-line string involved, every detection strategy built around inspecting a task's command line — including several of the queries in this pack — has nothing to match against. Confirming what a COM-handler task really runs means resolving its CLSID back to the registered handler in the registry, not reading the task definition itself.

procedure_examples.activity: Leveraged scheduled tasks via GPO to execute CaddyWiper during the 2022 Ukraine Electric Power Attack.
Employed schtasks for persistence, including periodic execution of remote XSL scripts.
Maintained persistence through scheduled task creation.
Established persistence using scheduled tasks alongside PowerShell Empire.
Used scheduled tasks as part of its self-propagation and persistence mechanism.

data_sources.detail: Scheduled task created / deleted / updated -- requires 'Audit Other Object Access Events' to be explicitly enabled.
Events 106 (created), 140 (updated), 141 (deleted), 200 (executed), 201 (execution completed) -- the fuller lifecycle, also not audited by default.
Process creation from svchost.exe or taskeng.exe as the parent, the typical execution-time signature of a fired scheduled task.

detection_queries.title: Scheduled Task Created with Suspicious Trigger or Action
detection_queries.description: Flags schtasks.exe task creation specifying an ONLOGON/ONSTART trigger paired with an executable in a non-standard path.
detection_queries.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("onlogon", "onstart", "/ru system")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

detection_queries.description: Flags schtasks.exe creating a task explicitly configured to run as SYSTEM, a common privilege-escalation pattern.

status: stable
author: H3AD-SEC Detection Engineering
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains: '/create'
  selection_ru:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '/ru'
      - 'system'
  condition: all of selection_*
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate administrative or deployment tooling that intentionally schedules SYSTEM-level maintenance tasks
level: medium
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - attack.t1053.005

false_positives: Legitimate software installers and deployment tooling that schedule SYSTEM-level maintenance or update-check tasks
IT-managed logon scripts and startup tasks that are a normal, documented part of the endpoint build
response_steps: Pull the full task definition (action, trigger, run-as context) via schtasks /query /tn <name> /xml

mitigations.name: Operating System Configuration
mitigations.detail: Configure tasks to run under an authenticated account context rather than SYSTEM where possible; disable 'Allow server operators to schedule tasks' via GPO.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Restrict 'Increase Scheduling Priority' rights to the Administrators group.

mitigations.name: User Account Management
mitigations.detail: Restrict remote task creation to authorized administrators; limit user privileges that enable escalation.

related.name: At
related.relation: The legacy scheduling mechanism this one superseded, still worth checking if schtasks activity alone comes up empty.

related.name: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
related.relation: Scheduled task creation is one of the two common execution triggers paired with an SMB-delivered payload.

hypothesis.statement: schtasks.exe creates a task with an ONLOGON or ONSTART trigger targeting an executable outside Program Files/Windows, or explicitly configured to run as SYSTEM.
hypothesis.rationale: Confirm Security 4698 and the Task Scheduler Operational log are both actually enabled in your environment before relying on this hypothesis -- neither is on by default, and a surprising number of environments assume this coverage exists without ever having turned it on.

subtechniques.name: Systemd Timers
subtechniques.overview: Systemd timers are .timer unit files that trigger a same-named .service unit on a calendar schedule or a time span relative to some starting point -- a more modern alternative to cron. System-wide timers live under /etc/systemd/system/ or /usr/lib/systemd/system/; user-level ones under ~/.config/systemd/user/.

concepts.term: A timer alone does nothing -- the pairing is the whole mechanism
concepts.explanation: A .timer file only defines a schedule; it has no payload of its own. It must be paired with a same-base-name .service file that defines what actually runs. A hunt built around 'new .timer file created' without also checking for its paired .service file is only seeing half the persistence mechanism and will miss exactly what the timer was set up to execute.

Because systemd itself runs as PID 1, any process it launches to fulfil a timer traces its parent lineage straight back to PID 1, running as root, regardless of which user actually created the timer/service pair. That's precisely the correlation MITRE's own detection strategy calls for: unit file creation or modification paired with abnormal child-process execution rooted at PID 1.

procedure_examples.activity: Registered itself as a systemd service on Kubernetes nodes to maintain persistence.
Created a gh-token-monitor daemon in a user systemd directory polling GitHub every 60 seconds, and a separate kitty-monitor.service for host persistence.

data_sources.detail: Creation or modification of .timer/.service files under /etc/systemd/system/, /usr/lib/systemd/system/, or ~/.config/systemd/user/.
A new process with PID 1 (systemd) as its parent, correlated against a recently created or modified timer/service pair.
systemd's own unit start/stop logging, which records exactly when a given .service fired and its exit status.

detection_queries.title: New Systemd Timer and Service Unit Pair
detection_queries.description: Flags creation of a .timer file alongside its paired .service file in a system-wide unit directory, outside of package-manager-driven installs.
detection_queries.query:
title: New Systemd Timer/Service Unit Created
id: 5b9d3e7a-2f4c-4a8e-9d6b-3f7a2c9e5d20
status: experimental
author: H3AD-SEC Detection Engineering
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.timer'
      - '.service'
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/etc/systemd/system/'
      - '/usr/lib/systemd/system/'
  filter_package_manager:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/dpkg'
      - '/rpm'
      - '/apt'
      - '/yum'
  condition: selection and not filter_package_manager
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate software installation via a package manager, which routinely drops new unit files as part of normal application setup
level: medium
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - attack.t1053.006

false_positives: Legitimate software installed via a package manager (apt/yum/dnf), which routinely creates its own .timer/.service pairs as part of normal setup
IT-managed configuration deployment (Ansible, Puppet) that legitimately templates systemd units as part of approved automation
response_steps: Locate and read both the .timer and its paired .service file to understand the schedule and the actual command
Check journalctl for that unit's execution history to establish how long it's been running and how often
Disable and remove both unit files (systemctl disable/stop then delete), not just the .timer
Check for the same unit name across other Linux hosts sharing a configuration-management baseline

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Restrict root access and prevent unauthorized creation or modification of systemd timer files.

mitigations.name: Restrict File and Directory Permissions
mitigations.detail: Limit read/write access to .timer unit files to authorized administrators.

mitigations.name: User Account Management
mitigations.detail: Control access to systemctl and systemd-run for legitimate users only.

related.name: Cron
related.relation: The older Linux scheduling mechanism systemd timers are increasingly used alongside or in place of.

hypothesis.statement: A new .timer file and its paired .service file appear under /etc/systemd/system/ or /usr/lib/systemd/system/ outside of a package-manager-driven install.
hypothesis.rationale: Exclude package-manager-initiated writes first -- most .timer/.service creation on a typical Linux host is entirely legitimate software installation, and without that exclusion this hunt drowns in noise before it reaches anything worth investigating.

subtechniques.name: Container Orchestration Job
subtechniques.overview: Kubernetes CronJobs schedule Jobs, which in turn run Pods, on a recurring basis -- the cluster-native equivalent of cron. Adversaries create a CronJob to redeploy a malicious container repeatedly across cluster nodes, giving them a persistence mechanism that survives individual pod restarts or even node rescheduling.

concepts.explanation: Kubernetes' own reconciliation loop exists to keep a desired number of replicas running at all times -- a legitimate reliability feature that becomes a persistence mechanism in reverse once a CronJob is redeploying a malicious pod. Killing that pod doesn't end the problem the way killing a process on a single host would: the cluster itself will actively work to bring it back, which is a fundamentally stronger persistence guarantee than anything else in this pack.

concepts.term: A cluster-wide concern, not a host-wide one
concepts.explanation: A single malicious CronJob object in the Kubernetes API can have its resulting pods scheduled onto whichever node the scheduler happens to pick -- containment has to happen at the API/RBAC layer (deleting the CronJob object itself, revoking the identity or service account that created it) rather than by cleaning up any one node, since the node that ran it today may not be the node it runs on tomorrow.

data_sources.detail: CronJob creation ('create' verb against the batch/v1 CronJob resource), especially by an identity outside the expected CI/CD or platform-team service accounts.
Job and Pod creation events attributable to a CronJob's controller reference, useful for tracing which CronJob actually spawned a given suspicious pod.

detection_queries.title: CronJob Created by Unexpected Identity
detection_queries.description: Flags creation of a Kubernetes CronJob object from an identity outside the platform's known CI/CD or automation service accounts.
detection_queries.query:
title: Kubernetes CronJob Created by Unexpected Identity
id: 9e6b4a8c-3f7d-4c2a-9d6e-8b3a9c7f4d40
status: experimental
author: H3AD-SEC Detection Engineering
logsource:
  category: application
  product: kubernetes
detection:
  selection:
    objectRef.resource: 'cronjobs'
    verb: 'create'
  filter_cicd:
    user.username|startswith: 'system:serviceaccount:ci-cd:'
  condition: selection and not filter_cicd
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate platform-team automation and CI/CD pipelines that create scheduled jobs as part of normal operations
level: medium
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - attack.t1053.007

false_positives: Legitimate platform-team automation, backup jobs, or CI/CD pipelines that create CronJobs as part of normal cluster operations
Scheduled maintenance jobs (log rotation, certificate renewal) deployed via Helm charts or GitOps tooling
response_steps: Delete the malicious CronJob object first, not just the currently-running pod -- otherwise the cluster will simply recreate it on the next scheduled interval
Identify and revoke the identity/service account that created it, and audit what else that identity has access to
Check the Job's pod spec for privileged container flags or hostPath mounts, which indicate a broader host-escape objective beyond just persistence
Review RBAC bindings that allowed CronJob creation by that identity in the first place, and scope them down

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Ensure containers are not running as root by default; define Pod Security Standards that prevent privileged containers.

mitigations.name: User Account Management
mitigations.detail: Restrict which identities can create orchestration jobs via RBAC, limited to authorized administrators and automation accounts.

related.name: Container CLI/API
related.relation: The same Kubernetes API surface, used here for scheduled persistence rather than interactive exec-based execution.

hypothesis.statement: A Kubernetes CronJob object is created by an identity outside the cluster's documented CI/CD or platform-automation service accounts, particularly one whose pod spec requests a privileged container or a hostPath mount.
hypothesis.rationale: Weight the privileged-container/hostPath detail heavily when triaging -- a CronJob without either is a persistence concern, but one with them is a far more urgent host-escape concern that should jump the queue.
